analysis.one_liner: Lets troops and civilians rape, sexually assaulted, or seriously injured by overseas contractors sue them in U.S. courts.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee approved the bill with bipartisan support and put it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies holding federal contracts worth $5 million or more performed outside the United States to agree in advance that they can be sued in U.S. federal courts if their employees rape, sexually assault, or seriously injure American troops, federal civilian workers, or American employees working under the contract. It would also let the government bar companies from future federal contracts if they dodge legal papers or skip court appearances. It passed through committee with an amendment but never came up for a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: American troops, federal civilian employees, and U.S. citizen employees of companies working under U.S. contracts overseas who are raped, sexually assaulted, or seriously injured by contractor personnel. Under current law these cases can fall into a gap where no U.S. court will hear them; this bill gives victims and their families a guaranteed courtroom in the United States, a designated U.S. agent to receive legal papers, and, in some cases, the application of state law from a hazardous-duty zone instead of foreign law. It also arms the government to debar contractors who evade lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Troops and civilians harmed by contractors

how_it_helps.text: Requires contractors on covered overseas federal contracts to consent to personal jurisdiction in federal courts, and specifically in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, in civil actions alleging rape, sexual assault, or serious bodily injury to a service member, federal civilian employee, or U.S. citizen contractor employee.
Requires contractors without a U.S. office to designate an agent in the United States for service of process, so victims can actually serve them with a lawsuit.

Provides that in civil suits arising in locations the Defense Secretary designates as hazardous duty zones, the law of a U.S. state applies rather than the law of the country where the incident occurred.
Permits the government to debar or suspend contractors who evade service of process or fail to appear in federal court in cases tied to their contract work.

analysis.who_pays: Government contractors performing work overseas, including their subsidiaries and subcontractors, which would face lawsuits in U.S. courts, compliance requirements, and possible debarment for dodging legal process. Some of those litigation and compliance costs could ultimately be passed through to taxpayers in contract prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to contracts entered into after its effective date, so people harmed under existing contracts would get no help from it.

The committee amendment narrowed the bill: the contract threshold was raised from $1 million to $5 million, and the requirement to consent to criminal prosecutions was dropped, leaving only civil actions brought by the United States under that section.
The bill does not create any new cause of action; it only guarantees a forum, so victims still need an underlying legal claim that supports a suit.
Contractors facing U.S.-court exposure for overseas incidents could seek higher contract prices, spreading some cost to taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a narrow, targeted fix to a real gap: Americans harmed by contractors the U.S. government itself hired could not reliably get into a U.S. courtroom. The costs are modest and mostly fall on the contractors being sued, though some may flow to taxpayers. The bill's own drafters diluted it in committee — a higher dollar threshold, prospective-only coverage, and no criminal-jurisdiction consent — so it helps future victims on large new contracts but not anyone already harmed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Homeland Security committee approved the bill favorably with an amendment and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the House never considered it.

narrative.text: Senator McCaskill introduced the bill on November 17, 2009, with cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
On April 28, 2010, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

On December 9, 2010, the committee reported the bill with an amendment that raised the contract-value threshold from $1 million to $5 million and narrowed the government-enforcement section to civil actions.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 682, but no floor vote ever occurred and no House action followed before the 111th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractors performing federal contracts overseas come out ahead: they never had to accept U.S. court jurisdiction over sexual assault and serious-injury claims, and they avoided debarment exposure for evading lawsuits. Victims on existing contracts are left where they started.

for.name: Claire McCaskill
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Joe Lieberman
for.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate with an amendment and placed it on the legislative calendar.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a floor vote; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support split across party lines: a Democratic sponsor and 6 Democratic cosponsors were joined by 3 Republican cosponsors, and the committee that reported the bill was chaired by an Independent; the bill's failure had no recorded opposition vote.

industries.industry: Overseas federal contractors (military support, security, and reconstruction firms)
industries.note: The bill would have let their victims — including troops alleging rape or serious injury — sue them in U.S. courts and let the government debar them for evading legal process. Their interest in avoiding that liability runs directly against the people the bill was written to protect.
